stem: Which FAR part covers competition requirements, including full and open competition and the exceptions to it?

options.text: FAR Part 6
options.why: Part 6, Competition Requirements, holds full and open competition (6.101), excluding sources (6.102) and the seven exceptions (6.103).

options.text: FAR Part 5
options.why: Part 5 is Publicizing Contract Actions: notices on SAM.gov, not the competition rules themselves.

options.text: FAR Part 10
options.why: Part 10 is Market Research.

options.text: FAR Part 13
options.why: Part 13 is Simplified Procedures for Noncommercial Acquisitions.

note: The class version said Part 13 holds all simplified acquisition procedures. Under the RFO, Part 13 covers only noncommercial buys at or below the SAT; commercial simplified procedures (up to $9 million) moved to FAR 12.201-1 and micro-purchases to subpart 12.4.
stem: You need to buy noncommercial items valued at $120,000 using simplified procedures. Which FAR part covers this buy?

options.text: FAR Part 13, Simplified Procedures for Noncommercial Acquisitions
options.why: Since the RFO, Part 13 applies only to noncommercial products and services above the micro-purchase threshold and at or below the SAT. It points you to the RFQ procedures in 12.201-1.

options.text: FAR Part 8, Required Sources of Supplies and Services
options.why: Part 8 tells you to check required sources first; it is not the simplified procedures part.

options.text: FAR Part 11, Describing Agency Needs
options.why: Part 11 is about writing the requirement, not the buying procedure.

options.text: FAR Part 14, Sealed Bidding
options.why: Sealed bidding is a formal method with public bid opening, not a simplified procedure.

stem: Which FAR part covers contracting by negotiation, including source selection?

options.text: FAR Part 15
options.why: Part 15, Contracting by Negotiation, covers requests for proposals, source selection, negotiations, debriefings and contract pricing. The exam FAQ tells you to read it thoroughly.

options.text: FAR Part 12
options.why: Part 12 covers commercial products and services.

options.text: FAR Part 14
options.why: Part 14 is Sealed Bidding: no negotiation at all.

options.text: FAR Part 16
options.why: Part 16 is Types of Contracts.

stem: A contractor wants to know where the FAR covers protests, disputes and appeals. Which part do you point to?

options.text: FAR Part 33
options.why: Part 33, Protests, Disputes, and Appeals: subpart 33.1 is protests and subpart 33.2 is disputes and appeals.

options.text: FAR Part 31
options.why: Part 31 is Contract Cost Principles and Procedures.

options.text: FAR Part 43
options.why: Part 43 is Contract Modifications.

options.text: FAR Part 49
options.why: Part 49 is Termination of Contracts.

stem: Which FAR part governs the acquisition of commercial products and commercial services?

options.text: FAR Part 12
options.why: Part 12, Acquisition of Commercial Products and Commercial Services. Since the RFO it also holds commercial simplified procedures (12.201-1) and micro-purchases (subpart 12.4).

options.text: FAR Part 10
options.why: Part 10 is Market Research, which tells you whether a need can be met commercially, but the buying rules are in Part 12.

options.text: FAR Part 11
options.why: Part 11 is Describing Agency Needs.

options.text: FAR Part 13
options.why: Part 13 now covers noncommercial simplified buys only.

stem: Where do you look for policy on acquisition planning?

options.text: FAR Part 7
options.why: Part 7, Acquisition Planning, covers acquisition plans and related planning duties.

options.text: FAR Part 6
options.why: Part 6 is Competition Requirements.

options.text: FAR Part 8
options.why: Part 8 is Required Sources of Supplies and Services.

options.text: FAR Part 9
options.why: Part 9 is Contractor Qualifications (responsibility, debarment, conflicts of interest).

stem: Which FAR part addresses contract modifications, including administrative changes and change orders?

options.text: FAR Part 43
options.why: Part 43, Contract Modifications: bilateral and unilateral modifications (43.203) and change orders (subpart 43.3).

options.text: FAR Part 33
options.why: Part 33 is Protests, Disputes, and Appeals.

options.text: FAR Part 44
options.why: Part 44 is Subcontracting Policies and Procedures.

options.text: FAR Part 46
options.why: Part 46 is Quality Assurance.

stem: Which FAR part discusses the types of contracts, such as fixed-price and cost-reimbursement?

options.text: FAR Part 16
options.why: Part 16, Types of Contracts: fixed-price (16.2), cost-reimbursement (16.3), incentive (16.4), indefinite-delivery (16.5) and more.

options.text: FAR Part 17
options.why: Part 17 is Special Contracting Methods, such as options and multiyear contracts.

options.text: FAR Part 18
options.why: Part 18 covers emergency acquisitions.

options.text: FAR Part 22
options.why: Part 22 covers labor laws in Government contracts.

stem: Which FAR part addresses termination of contracts?

options.text: FAR Part 49
options.why: Part 49, Termination of Contracts, covers termination for convenience and for default. Commercial contracts use FAR 12.304 and 52.212-4 instead.

options.text: FAR Part 33
options.why: Part 33 covers protests and disputes; a default termination can lead to a dispute, but the termination rules are in Part 49.

options.text: FAR Part 37
options.why: Part 37 is Service Contracting.

options.text: FAR Part 52
options.why: Part 52 holds the clause text, including the termination clauses, but the policy is in Part 49.

stem: Which FAR part covers small business set-asides, 8(a), HUBZone, SDVOSB and WOSB programs?

options.text: FAR Part 19
options.why: Part 19. Its RFO title is simply "Small Business" (it was "Small Business Programs").

options.text: FAR Part 6
options.why: Part 6 allows set-asides as competition after excluding sources (6.102-2) but sends you to Part 19 for the programs.

options.text: FAR Part 12
options.why: Part 12 covers commercial buys.

options.text: FAR Part 25
options.why: Part 25 is Foreign Acquisition.

stem: Which FAR part covers market research?

options.text: FAR Part 10
options.why: Part 10, Market Research. Since the RFO it is one short section (10.001) that sets when market research is required.

options.text: FAR Part 6
options.why: Part 6 is Competition Requirements.

options.text: FAR Part 19
options.why: Part 19 is Small Business.

options.text: FAR Part 25
options.why: Part 25 is Foreign Acquisition.

stem: Which FAR part covers the Federal Acquisition Regulations System itself: guiding principles, deviations and contracting officer authority?

options.text: FAR Part 1
options.why: Part 1 covers the framework, guiding principles (1.102), conventions (1.107), deviations (subpart 1.3) and contracting authority (subpart 1.4).

options.text: FAR Part 2
options.why: Part 2 holds definitions.

options.text: FAR Part 4
options.why: Part 4 is Administrative and Information Matters.

options.text: FAR Part 46
options.why: Part 46 is Quality Assurance.

stem: Which FAR part covers sealed bidding, including public bid opening and award?

options.text: FAR Part 14
options.why: Part 14, Sealed Bidding: invitations for bids, public opening (14.303) and award to the responsible bidder whose conforming bid is most advantageous on price and price-related factors (14.307).

options.text: FAR Part 13
options.why: Part 13 is simplified procedures for noncommercial buys.

options.text: FAR Part 15
options.why: Part 15 is negotiation.

options.text: FAR Part 12
options.why: Part 12 is commercial buys.

note: The class version cited FAR 6.302-1. The RFO moved this authority to FAR 6.103-1.
stem: Only one company has ever built a specialized radar calibration system that meets DoW specifications. The requiring activity wants a sole-source award. Which reason supports other than full and open competition?

options.text: Only one responsible source can satisfy the agency's requirements, and no other supplies or services will do
options.why: That is the first statutory exception (FAR 6.103-1). For DoW it also covers a limited number of responsible sources. It still needs a justification and approval (6.104).

options.text: The requiring activity prefers that contractor
options.why: Preference is not a statutory exception.

options.text: The contractor won the last contract
options.why: Being the incumbent alone does not justify limiting competition.

options.text: The contractor has already started preliminary work
options.why: Work begun without a contract is an unauthorized commitment problem, not a justification. Lack of planning can never justify a sole-source award (6.103(b)).

note: The class version cited FAR 6.302-2 and FedBizOpps. The RFO moved urgency to FAR 6.103-2, which now says the justification may be completed after award if doing it first would unreasonably delay the buy. FedBizOpps was replaced by SAM.gov in 2019.
stem: A mission-critical system overseas failed and the commander needs a replacement immediately. You plan to use the unusual and compelling urgency exception. What must you do?

options.text: Justify the exception in writing and get it approved; under urgency the justification may be completed after award if doing it first would unreasonably delay the buy
options.why: Urgency still needs a justification and approval (6.104), but 6.103-2(d) lets it be done after award. Solicit as many sources as practicable (6.103(c)) and keep the period of performance to what the urgency requires (no more than one year unless the agency head decides otherwise).

options.text: Award immediately; urgency removes the documentation requirements
options.why: Urgency changes the timing of the paperwork, not the requirement for it.

options.text: Use oral communications only and document nothing
options.why: Every action needs a complete file (FAR 4.101).

options.text: Post a presolicitation notice on SAM.gov and wait 15 days before awarding
options.why: When you use an other-than-full-and-open exception other than 6.103-1 or 6.103-6, a presolicitation notice is not required (FAR 5.101(b)(2)). Waiting would defeat the urgency.

stem: Your office plans a $50 million, five-year technical support services contract. The program manager wants a sole-source award because the incumbent knows the work. What does the Competition in Contracting Act require?

options.text: Full and open competition, unless a properly justified statutory exception applies
options.why: CICA requires competitive procedures (6.101). Familiarity alone is not an exception, and lack of planning can never justify a sole-source award (6.103(b)).

options.text: Award may proceed without competition because the contractor has experience
options.why: Experience is something to evaluate in a competition, not a reason to skip it.

options.text: Sole-source contracts under $100 million are automatically exempt
options.why: No dollar value makes a contract automatically exempt from competition; higher values need higher approval levels.

options.text: CICA does not apply to service contracts
options.why: CICA applies to supplies and services alike.

note: The class version cited FAR 6.303-1(c). Under the RFO, class justifications are in FAR 6.104(c) and their approval in 6.104-2(b).
stem: Your command will buy a proprietary encryption device from its only manufacturer several times over three years. Instead of a new justification for each buy, you are asked to prepare a class justification. Which statement is true?

options.text: A class justification can cover multiple contracts or orders with the same basis, approved at the level set by the class's total estimated value
options.why: Justifications under 6.103 (except public interest) may be made on an individual or class basis (6.104(c)); the estimated total value of the class sets the approval level (6.104-2(b)).

options.text: Class justifications are not allowed for DoW buys over $10 million
options.why: No such limit exists; the value sets the approval level.

options.text: Once approved, a program office can reuse it for anything without further approval
options.why: It covers only the defined class of actions and their estimated value.

options.text: Class justifications apply only to construction
options.why: They apply to any supplies or services.

note: The class version asked whether a sole-source justification is always required (True). That is not always so: two exceptions do not need a justification and approval. Rewritten to teach the exceptions.
stem: Which other-than-full-and-open authority does NOT require a justification and approval under FAR 6.104?

options.text: Authorized or required by statute (6.103-5), such as a sole-source 8(a) award under $30 million
options.why: 6.104(a) excludes 6.103-5 and 6.103-7. Public interest (6.103-7) needs an agency-head determination and notice to Congress instead. A sole-source 8(a) award over $30 million does need a justification.

options.text: Only one responsible source (6.103-1)
options.why: This is the most common exception and always needs a justification and approval.

options.text: Unusual and compelling urgency (6.103-2)
options.why: Urgency needs a justification, though it may be completed after award.

options.text: National security (6.103-6)
options.why: National security needs a justification and approval.

note: The class version cited FAR 8.405-6. Under the RFO, FAR 8.401(b) sends Federal Supply Schedule ordering to GSA's procedures in GSAR subpart 538.71, which keep the limited-sources justification.
stem: You are placing an order under a GSA Federal Supply Schedule. Market research shows only one schedule vendor can provide the exact service in the time needed. What do you prepare?

options.text: A limited-sources justification under the GSA schedule ordering procedures, not a FAR Part 6 justification
options.why: Schedule orders follow GSA's ordering procedures (FAR 8.401(b), GSAR 538.71). Restricting competition among schedule holders is supported by a limited-sources justification.

options.text: Nothing; schedule orders never need a justification
options.why: Limiting competition among schedule holders must be justified.

options.text: A Part 6 justification approved by the head of the contracting activity
options.why: Part 6 justifications are for open-market contracts, not schedule orders.

options.text: Cancel the requirement until more vendors appear
options.why: The need is real; document the reason and proceed properly.

note: The class version cited FAR 15.304 and 15.305. Under the RFO the rules are in FAR 15.104 (evaluation factors) and 15.201 and 15.202 (evaluate only on the stated factors).
stem: During an IT services source selection, your technical team wants to score offerors on new criteria that are not in the RFP. What do you tell them?

options.text: No. Proposals may be evaluated only on the factors and subfactors stated in the RFP
options.why: All factors that affect award must be stated in the RFP (15.104(a)), and the source selection authority must make sure proposals are evaluated solely on them (15.201(b)(4), 15.202(a)(1)). To add a factor you must amend the RFP and let offerors respond.

options.text: Yes, if the new criteria make the evaluation more objective
options.why: Objectivity does not cure undisclosed criteria; offerors had no chance to address them.

options.text: Score them internally but do not tell the offerors
options.why: Secret criteria are exactly what the rule forbids, and a protest would likely be sustained.

options.text: Add them after proposals arrive without telling anyone
options.why: Changes to evaluation criteria require an amendment to everyone still in the competition (15.106).

note: The class version cited FAR 15.404. The RFO kept price analysis at 15.404-1 and added that price analysis must be used whenever certified cost or pricing data are not required (15.404(a)(2)).
stem: On a firm-fixed-price commercial supply buy, one offer is far lower than the rest. Which analysis do you use to decide whether the price is fair and reasonable?

options.text: Price analysis, such as comparing the offers with each other and with prior or market prices
options.why: Price analysis must be used when certified cost or pricing data are not required (15.404(a)(2)), and commercial buys are exempt from certified data. Comparing competing offers and historical prices are the preferred techniques (15.404-1(c)).

options.text: Cost realism analysis, because the price seems too low
options.why: Cost realism is required for cost-reimbursement contracts; on a fixed-price buy it is optional and tests understanding, not reasonableness.

options.text: Cost analysis of each cost element
options.why: Cost analysis is required when certified cost or pricing data are required, which they are not here.

options.text: Technical analysis of the delivery schedule
options.why: Technical analysis supports cost or price analysis; it does not decide price reasonableness by itself.

note: The class version cited FAR 15.308. The RFO moved the source selection decision to FAR 15.205.
stem: In a tradeoff source selection, the team picked the highest-rated offeror, which was not the lowest priced. What must the source selection decision document include?

options.text: The rationale for the tradeoff, including the benefits that justify paying the higher price
options.why: The decision must show the SSA's independent judgment and the rationale for business judgments and tradeoffs, including benefits of the additional cost. It need not quantify the tradeoff (15.205).

options.text: Only why the selected offeror was technically acceptable
options.why: Acceptability is the LPTA question; a tradeoff needs a comparative rationale.

options.text: Only the price analysis
options.why: Price reasonableness is required too, but it does not explain the tradeoff.

options.text: Technical superiority alone, with no mention of price
options.why: A tradeoff weighs price against non-price factors; ignoring price is not a tradeoff.

note: The class version named the exchange "clarifications" under FAR 15.306(a). The RFO keeps clarifications (FAR 15.202(a)(2)) and allows them at any time after receipt of proposals through award.
stem: A proposal is acceptable overall but has an obvious clerical mistake in the price schedule. You want to resolve it without negotiating. What do you use?

options.text: Clarifications
options.why: Clarifications let an offeror resolve minor or clerical errors without revising its proposal (15.202(a)(2)). They do not open negotiations.

options.text: Negotiations with every offeror
options.why: Negotiations (formerly called discussions) let offerors revise proposals and require a competitive range.

options.text: Reject the proposal as nonresponsive
options.why: Responsiveness is a sealed-bidding idea, and a clerical error does not make a proposal unacceptable.

options.text: Evaluate it as submitted and assume the error was intentional
options.why: Clarifications exist so obvious errors do not decide the competition.

note: The class version described the competitive range as "all of the most highly rated proposals" (old FAR 15.306(c)). The RFO defines it as the proposals best suited for further negotiation (FAR 15.204-1) and calls discussions "negotiations".
stem: After initial evaluation, two offerors are technically unacceptable but much lower priced. Both say they could fix their proposals in negotiations. What is your best course of action?

options.text: Leave them out of the competitive range if their proposals are not among those best suited for further negotiation, regardless of price
options.why: The competitive range is the group of evaluated proposals best suited for further negotiation, and you may limit it to the most highly rated for an efficient competition (15.204-1). Send written notice to those excluded (15.206-1(a)).

options.text: Include them, because negotiations could fix their deficiencies
options.why: Including unacceptable proposals just because they might be fixed is not required and wastes everyone's time.

options.text: Include every offeror to maximize competition
options.why: The RFO lets you narrow the range for efficiency.

options.text: Award to the lowest price to get best value
options.why: A technically unacceptable proposal cannot be the best value.

note: The class version said discussions must be held with offerors in the competitive range (old FAR 15.306(d)). The RFO calls them negotiations (FAR 15.204-2) and requires at least raising deficiencies and significant weaknesses.
stem: You decide to negotiate after evaluating IT support proposals. What must you make sure of?

options.text: You negotiate with each responsible offeror in the competitive range and, at a minimum, raise its deficiencies and significant weaknesses
options.why: 15.204-2(b) requires negotiating with each responsible offeror in the range, tailored to its proposal. Then each one left in the range gets an equal chance to submit a written proposal revision (15.204-2(d)).

options.text: You discuss price only; technical proposals cannot change
options.why: Negotiations let offerors revise any part of their proposals.

options.text: You negotiate with every offeror, including those outside the competitive range
options.why: Negotiations are held with offerors in the competitive range.

options.text: Only the COR may conduct negotiations
options.why: The contracting officer controls all exchanges after receipt of proposals (15.201(c)(2)).

stem: During evaluation, an offeror calls to ask how its proposal is doing and offers more information to strengthen it. How do you respond?

options.text: Politely decline: the proposal cannot be revised now, and you share no evaluation status
options.why: After receipt of proposals the contracting officer controls all exchanges (15.201(c)(2)). Offerors may revise only when you ask for proposal revisions after negotiations; you may not reveal evaluation results early.

options.text: Accept the information so the evaluation is fair
options.why: Accepting unsolicited revisions from one offeror is unfair to the others.

options.text: Share how the competing proposals compare, for context
options.why: That would reveal source selection information (FAR 3.104).

options.text: Tell them to withdraw and resubmit a new proposal
options.why: A resubmission after the closing time would be late.

stem: What is the primary objective of the tradeoff approach in source selection?

options.text: To balance price against non-price factors to get the best value
options.why: The tradeoff approach allows award to other than the lowest priced or highest rated offeror when the benefits of a higher price merit the cost (15.103-1).

options.text: To select the lowest priced offer
options.why: That describes LPTA among acceptable proposals, not a tradeoff.

options.text: To speed up the procurement
options.why: Tradeoffs often take longer than LPTA.

options.text: To meet small business goals
options.why: Small business goals are handled through Part 19, not the tradeoff approach.

note: The class version listed a "best value continuum" option. The RFO replaced that idea with named approaches in FAR 15.103: tradeoff, LPTA, highest technically rated with a fair and reasonable price, and phased acquisition.
stem: Which of these is NOT a source selection approach under FAR Part 15?

options.text: Sealed bidding
options.why: Sealed bidding is its own procedure under Part 14, not a Part 15 source selection approach.

options.text: Lowest price technically acceptable
options.why: LPTA is a Part 15 approach (15.103-2).

options.text: Tradeoff
options.why: Tradeoff is a Part 15 approach (15.103-1).

options.text: Highest technically rated with a fair and reasonable price
options.why: This approach was added by the RFO (15.103-3): pick the top-rated proposal if its price is fair and reasonable, with no tradeoffs.

stem: Which is a key early step in a Part 15 source selection?

options.text: Defining the evaluation factors and their relative importance
options.why: Factors and their relative importance must be set and stated in the RFP before proposals arrive (15.104).

options.text: Monitoring contractor performance
options.why: That is contract administration after award.

options.text: Developing the statement of work
options.why: The requirement comes from the requiring activity during planning; it is not a source selection step.

options.text: Paying invoices
options.why: Payment happens after award and acceptance.

stem: You want proposals evaluated fairly and consistently. What is the best approach?

options.text: Establish an evaluation team with the right mix of expertise
options.why: The source selection authority establishes an evaluation team tailored to the acquisition, with contracting, legal, logistics, technical and other expertise (15.201(b)(1)).

options.text: Have one evaluator review every proposal
options.why: One person rarely has all the expertise a comprehensive evaluation needs.

options.text: Look only at price
options.why: Every competitive source selection must also evaluate quality (15.104(b)(2)).

options.text: Keep the evaluation criteria flexible
options.why: Criteria must be stated in the RFP and applied as written.

note: Same answer as the class version; the cite moved from FAR 15.308 to 15.205.
stem: What is the document that records the source selection authority's decision and rationale commonly called?

options.text: Source selection decision document (SSDD)
options.why: The source selection decision must be documented, including the rationale for tradeoffs (15.205). DoW calls it the SSDD and, for large awards, discloses a redacted copy in debriefings (15.301-1(c)).

options.text: Source selection plan
options.why: The plan is written before the RFP and sets how the evaluation will run.

options.text: Determination and findings
options.why: A D&F supports specific actions the FAR names, such as a T&M contract (FAR 1.501).

options.text: Price negotiation memorandum
options.why: The PNM documents a negotiated price (15.408-2).

stem: During evaluation of a software development RFP, you see that one proposal fails a minimum technical requirement but offers a much lower price. What do you do?

options.text: Treat it as having a deficiency; it cannot be selected unless the deficiency is corrected in negotiations
options.why: A deficiency is a failure to meet a material requirement (15.001). A proposal with one is unacceptable as submitted. If you hold negotiations and the offeror is in the competitive range, you must raise it (15.204-2).

options.text: Award to it because it has the lowest price
options.why: An unacceptable proposal cannot be the best value.

options.text: Quietly negotiate with that offeror alone
options.why: Negotiations require a competitive range and must be held with each offeror in it.

options.text: Reissue the RFP with lower requirements so it can win
options.why: Change requirements only when the Government's need changes, not to help one offeror.

stem: Your agency needs a complex IT system for several departments and wants detailed technical proposals. Which method fits best?

options.text: Negotiated procurement (competitive proposals under Part 15)
options.why: Complex buys where you must evaluate technical approaches and may need to negotiate call for competitive proposals (6.101(b)(2)).

options.text: Sealed bidding
options.why: Sealed bidding works only when award is on price and price-related factors and no discussion is needed (6.101(b)(1)).

options.text: Simplified procedures
options.why: A complex multi-department system would far exceed simplified thresholds and needs detailed evaluation.

options.text: Micro-purchase
options.why: Micro-purchases are at or below $15,000.

stem: You issued an IFB for base construction. Five timely, responsive bids arrived and the low bidder is responsible. Your technical evaluator likes a higher-priced bid's performance better. What do you do?

options.text: Award to the responsible bidder whose conforming bid is lowest on price and price-related factors
options.why: Sealed bidding awards only on price and price-related factors (14.307(a)(3)). Quality is handled through the specifications and responsibility, not a tradeoff.

options.text: Award to the higher-priced bid with better performance
options.why: That is a tradeoff, which sealed bidding does not allow.

options.text: Convert to a negotiated procurement now
options.why: You may not change methods to avoid awarding to a proper low bid.

options.text: Cancel the IFB and start a tradeoff under Part 15
options.why: Cancelling after opening needs a compelling reason (14.305); preferring a higher price is not one.

stem: Which step is a key part of sealed bidding?

options.text: Publicly opening the bids at the set time
options.why: The bid opening officer personally and publicly opens all timely bids and, if practical, reads them aloud (14.303(c)).

options.text: Issuing a request for proposals
options.why: An RFP is the Part 15 solicitation; sealed bidding uses an invitation for bids.

options.text: Negotiating with bidders
options.why: Sealed bidding does not allow negotiation.

options.text: Evaluating past performance
options.why: Past performance can bear on responsibility, but it is not an evaluation factor in sealed bidding.

stem: What is the purpose of a request for proposals (RFP)?

options.text: To invite offerors to submit proposals for a specific requirement
options.why: RFPs communicate the Government's requirement and request proposals in negotiated acquisitions (15.100).

options.text: To solicit sealed bids for construction
options.why: Sealed bids are requested with an invitation for bids.

options.text: To gather information for planning only
options.why: That is a request for information (15.101(c)).

options.text: To announce a contract award
options.why: Awards are announced with award notices (subpart 5.3).

stem: What is the purpose of a request for information (RFI)?

options.text: To gather price, delivery, market or capability information for planning when no award is intended yet
options.why: RFIs are for planning. Responses are not offers and cannot be accepted to form a contract (15.101(c)).

options.text: To solicit formal bids
options.why: Bids are requested with an IFB.

options.text: To award a contract
options.why: The Government cannot award based on an RFI.

options.text: To protest an award
options.why: Protests are filed under Part 33.

note: The class version said an RFQ "is not an offer" and an RFP "is an offer". Strictly, both are solicitations; it is the responses that differ: a quotation is not an offer, a proposal is. Under the RFO this is in FAR 12.201-1(b) and 2.101.
stem: What is the key legal difference between a response to an RFQ and a response to an RFP?

options.text: A quotation is not an offer, so the Government cannot accept it; a proposal is an offer the Government can accept
options.why: Neither a quotation nor the purchase order issued in response forms a contract; the order is the Government's offer, and the contract forms when the supplier accepts in writing or by substantial performance (12.201-1(b)).

options.text: RFPs ask for price; RFQs ask only for technical capability
options.why: Both usually ask for price.

options.text: RFPs are for services and RFQs are for supplies
options.why: Either can be used for supplies or services.

options.text: There is no difference
options.why: The offer-or-not difference decides when a binding contract forms.

stem: You issued an RFP last week. The performance work statement has now changed because the requirement was clarified. What do you do?

options.text: Issue an amendment to the solicitation
options.why: When the Government changes its requirements or terms, the contracting officer must amend the RFP; before the closing date it goes to everyone who received the RFP (15.106(a)).

options.text: Issue a unilateral contract modification
options.why: There is no contract yet; modifications change awarded contracts.

options.text: Issue a bilateral contract modification
options.why: Same problem: no contract exists yet.

options.text: Always cancel and start over
options.why: Cancel only when the change is so substantial that others would likely have competed had they known (15.106(e)(2)).

stem: Proposals are due 15 March. On 12 March you learn something that requires clarifying the evaluation criteria. What complies with the FAR?

options.text: Issue an amendment that revises the criteria and extends the due date so offerors can respond
options.why: Changes before closing go to everyone who received the RFP (15.106(a)(1)), with a revised closing date when needed (15.106(b)(7)).

options.text: Issue a contract modification
options.why: Modifications are for awarded contracts.

options.text: Tell only the apparent low offeror
options.why: Every prospective offeror must get the same information.

options.text: Cancel the solicitation and begin again
options.why: An amendment fixes this; cancelling wastes everyone's effort.

note: Same answer as the class version; under the RFO the RFQ procedures are in FAR 12.201-1 and evaluation in 12.203.
stem: After quotations arrive on a logistics support RFQ, you find an error in the PWS that could materially affect pricing. What do you do?

options.text: Amend the RFQ and give every quoter a chance to revise its quotation
options.why: A material error must be fixed for everyone. Under simplified procedures you may solicit revised quotations without a competitive range (12.203(c)(2)).

options.text: Award to the lowest quote and fix the PWS after award
options.why: Quoters priced the wrong work; fixing it later invites claims and protests.

options.text: Always cancel and issue a new RFQ
options.why: An amendment usually solves it faster.

options.text: Award on best value and tell the others afterward
options.why: That leaves everyone pricing a flawed requirement.

note: The class version asked about an $80,000 RFQ under FAR 13.104 and 13.106. Under the RFO, soliciting directly at or below the SAT is in FAR 12.201-1(c)(2): post a notice unless an exemption applies and solicit at least three sources.
stem: You plan to email an RFQ for $80,000 of commercial maintenance equipment directly to four vendors found in market research instead of posting it. What do the RFO rules require?

options.text: Promote competition: post a presolicitation notice unless an exemption applies, solicit at least three sources, and document the award
options.why: When you solicit directly at or below the SAT you must post a notice under subpart 5.1 unless exempt, solicit at least three sources and, when practicable, two not used last time (12.201-1(c)(2)). Document the procedures and quotes received (12.204(b)(1)).

options.text: Post the RFQ publicly no matter what
options.why: Direct solicitation is allowed at or below the SAT.

options.text: Get at least five quotes
options.why: The RFO sets three sources when soliciting directly, not five.

options.text: Only one quote is needed under simplified procedures
options.why: Soliciting one source needs a documented reason (12.102(a)).

note: The class version cited FAR 13.106-2. Under the RFO, evaluation of quotations is in FAR 12.203 and award documentation in 12.204(b).
stem: Under simplified procedures you received three quotes. The lowest has questionable past performance; the highest has excellent performance and a strong technical solution. You want a best-value award. What must you do?

options.text: Award to the quote that is the best value, as the RFQ said you would evaluate, and document the basis
options.why: Tell quoters the basis for award (12.203(b)), use broad discretion in evaluating (12.203(c)(2)), and put a written description of the procedures and quotes received in the file (12.204(b)(1)).

options.text: Award to the lowest price regardless of performance
options.why: Simplified procedures allow best-value decisions when the RFQ says so.

options.text: Award on discretion with no documentation
options.why: The file must describe how the award was made.

options.text: Recompete under Part 15
options.why: Simplified procedures already allow this decision.

note: The class version cited FAR 13.106-3 and a $150,000 figure. Under the RFO, FAR 12.203(c)(2) says you need not have evaluation plans, scores or a competitive range for quotations, and the SAT is now $350,000.
stem: You awarded a $175,000 commercial buy under simplified procedures on technical merit and past performance. A new specialist asks why there was no formal source selection plan or board. What is the correct answer?

options.text: Simplified procedures do not require evaluation plans or boards; the contracting officer documents the basis for award
options.why: Contracting officers are not required to have evaluation plans, score quotations or set a competitive range (12.203(c)(2)), but must document the procedures used (12.204(b)(1)).

options.text: Simplified procedures require a formal plan above $150,000
options.why: No such rule exists.

options.text: Only DCAA can approve source selection plans
options.why: DCAA audits contractors; it does not approve source selection plans.

options.text: A board is required when more than three quotes arrive
options.why: No such rule exists.

note: The class version said simplified procedures could be used under the old FAR 13.500 threshold. Under the RFO, FAR 12.200(a) and 10.001(f) tell you to buy from an existing governmentwide contract, such as a GSA Schedule, first when it meets the need.
stem: You must buy commercial IT support services worth $230,000. Market research shows several GSA Schedule holders offer them. What do the RFO rules point you to first?

options.text: Buy through the existing governmentwide contract (the GSA Schedule) if it meets the need
options.why: If commercial products or services are available from a priority source in Part 8, including Federal Supply Schedules, procure from that source; if not, use Part 12's streamlined procedures (12.200(a)). Market research checks existing governmentwide contracts first (10.001(f)(1)).

options.text: Simplified procedures cannot be used for services
options.why: Simplified procedures cover supplies and services.

options.text: It must be a sole-source buy to use simplified procedures
options.why: Simplified procedures are competitive by default.

options.text: It must go to Part 15 because it is over $250,000
options.why: The SAT is now $350,000 and commercial simplified procedures reach $9 million.

note: The class version said commercial simplified procedures stop at $7.5 million. The October 2025 inflation adjustment and the RFO set it at $9 million (FAR 12.201-1), or $15 million for the special cases in 12.001(c).
stem: Up to what value may you use simplified procedures (RFQ, then purchase order) for commercial products and services?

options.text: $9 million ($15 million for contingency, disaster and attack-related buys)
options.why: 12.201-1(a) sets $9 million; 12.001(c) raises it to $15 million for contingency operations, defense against or recovery from attacks, international disaster assistance, and emergencies or major disasters.

options.text: $7.5 million
options.why: That was the figure before the October 2025 inflation adjustment.
That is the simplified acquisition threshold, which caps noncommercial simplified buys under Part 13.

options.text: $1 million
options.why: That is the contingency SAT inside the United States.

note: Same answer as the class version; under the RFO, BPAs are described in FAR 12.201-1(e)(3).
stem: What is the purpose of a blanket purchase agreement (BPA)?

options.text: To fill anticipated repetitive needs by setting up "charge accounts" with qualified sources
options.why: A BPA obligates the Government only when authorized orders are placed (12.201-1(e)(3)). It does not justify sole-sourcing or skipping set-asides.

options.text: To create a long-term contract that obligates funds at signing
options.why: A BPA is not a contract and obligates nothing until an order is placed.

options.text: To negotiate terms with many suppliers at once
options.why: BPAs may be with several suppliers, but their purpose is simple repeat buying.

options.text: To terminate an existing contract
options.why: Terminations are under Part 49 or 12.304.

stem: Which instrument is the normal way to buy under simplified procedures?

options.text: A purchase order issued after a request for quotations
options.why: Simplified procedures issue an RFQ followed by a purchase order (12.201-1(a)); Part 13 uses the same procedures for noncommercial buys (13.201).

options.text: Sealed bidding
options.why: Sealed bidding is Part 14.

options.text: A request for proposals
options.why: RFPs are used above $9 million for commercial buys (12.201-2) or under Part 15.

options.text: An indefinite-delivery contract
options.why: That is a contract type under Part 16.

note: The class version asked about oral quotations under the old FAR 13.106-1. The RFO dropped that text from Parts 12 and 13, so the rewritten question uses the oral RFP rule that is still in FAR 15.102(b)(1)(ii).
stem: When may a contracting officer use an oral RFP under the RFO version of Part 15?

options.text: When a written RFP would delay the buy to the Government's detriment and the RFP is not required to be posted under Part 5
options.why: RFPs may be written or oral (15.102(a)); oral RFPs fit when processing a written one would cause harmful delay and no posting is required (15.102(b)(1)(ii)). Keep a good record in the file.

options.text: Never; every RFP must be written
options.why: The RFO expressly allows oral RFPs in the right circumstances.

options.text: Only below the micro-purchase threshold
options.why: Micro-purchases need no RFP at all.

options.text: Only for construction
options.why: Nothing limits oral RFPs to construction.

note: The class version cited FAR 12.403 for commercial terminations. Under the RFO the procedures are in FAR 12.304, and it says not to use Part 49.
stem: You are terminating a contract for commercial off-the-shelf equipment for convenience because the mission changed. What process do you follow?

options.text: Follow FAR 12.304 and paragraph (l) of 52.212-4; the parties agree on a simple termination proposal, not a Part 49 settlement
options.why: For commercial contracts, follow 12.304 and the termination paragraphs of 52.212-4, and do not use Part 49 (12.304(a)). The contractor gets a percentage of the price for work done plus reasonable charges resulting from the termination.

options.text: Use a full Part 49 settlement with cost accounting
options.why: 12.304(a) says not to use Part 49 procedures for commercial contracts.

options.text: Convert it to a default termination to avoid paying anything
options.why: Default needs contractor fault; misusing it would be converted to convenience anyway.

options.text: Demand a certified settlement proposal on Part 49 forms
options.why: The commercial clause says the contractor need not use cost principles or cost accounting standards.

note: The class version asked how to "end" a contract awarded on SF 1449 without saying why. Rewritten to give the reason (failure to deliver), which decides the answer.
stem: You awarded a commercial contract on an SF 1449 and the contractor has failed to deliver. Which termination applies?

options.text: Termination for cause under 52.212-4(m)
options.why: Commercial contracts are terminated for cause, not default. Send a cure notice first unless the reason is late delivery (12.304(b)(1)).

options.text: Termination for default under Part 49
options.why: Default terminations under Part 49 are for noncommercial contracts.

options.text: Termination for convenience
options.why: The contractor is at fault, so convenience is not the right remedy.

options.text: A no-cost stop-work order
options.why: A stop-work order pauses work; it does not end the contract for failure to deliver.

note: The class version assumed an SF 1442 always means a noncommercial contract. Under the RFO, construction can be bought as a commercial service (FAR 12.200(b)), so the question now says the contract is noncommercial.
stem: A noncommercial construction contract awarded on an SF 1442 must be ended because the contractor defaulted. Which termination applies?

options.text: Termination for default under FAR Part 49
options.why: Noncommercial contracts are terminated for default under Part 49 and the Default clause (52.249-10 for construction).

options.text: Termination for cause, because construction is commercial
options.why: Termination for cause is for commercial contracts; this one is noncommercial.

options.text: Termination for convenience
options.why: The contractor defaulted, so convenience is not the right remedy.

options.text: Termination for delay
options.why: There is no such termination type.

stem: A construction contractor failed to mobilize by the start date. Plenty of time remains before completion, and you want to give it a chance to fix the problem first. What is the first step?

options.text: Issue a cure notice giving at least 10 days to fix the failure
options.why: For failures that endanger performance, give written notice and at least 10 days to cure (49.402-3(d)). If fewer than 10 days remain, a show cause notice is used instead.

options.text: Issue a show cause notice immediately
options.why: A show cause notice is used when there is not enough time left for a realistic 10-day cure.

options.text: Suspend the contract and start legal action
options.why: Legal action is not a first step.

options.text: Terminate for default right away
options.why: Failure to make progress needs notice and a chance to cure first.

stem: Which is a reason for a termination for convenience?

options.text: The Government no longer needs the supplies or services
options.why: Convenience terminations end work the Government no longer needs, without contractor fault.

options.text: The contractor failed to perform
options.why: That leads to default (or cause, for commercial contracts).

options.text: The contractor breached the contract
options.why: Breach is the contractor's fault: default or cause.

options.text: The contractor went bankrupt
options.why: Bankruptcy has its own procedures (subpart 42.7).

stem: You have decided to terminate a contract for convenience. What is one of your first steps?

options.text: Notify the contractor in writing with a notice of termination
options.why: Terminations start with a written notice that states the effective date and extent (49.102).

options.text: Stop all payments immediately
options.why: The contractor is owed payment for accepted work and a fair settlement.

options.text: Demand a refund
options.why: A convenience termination does not entitle the Government to a refund.

options.text: Hire a new contractor immediately
options.why: If the need is gone, there is nothing to rebuy.

stem: After a convenience termination, the contractor sends a settlement proposal. What is your role?

options.text: Negotiate a fair settlement with the contractor
options.why: Settlement should compensate the contractor fairly for work done and preparations made, by negotiated agreement where possible (49.103, 49.201).

options.text: Reject it outright
options.why: The contractor is entitled to a fair settlement.

options.text: Send it to the agency head
options.why: The termination contracting officer handles the settlement.

options.text: Ignore it and close the contract
options.why: Do not close a contract until termination actions are complete (4.308-2(d)).

note: The class version offered vague choices ("profit margin" or "incurred costs"). Rewritten so the right answer shows the full settlement formula and the wrong ones show what is never paid.
stem: You are settling a fixed-price contract terminated for convenience. Which items does a fair settlement normally include?

options.text: Costs incurred on the terminated work, a reasonable profit on work done (unless the contractor would have lost money), and settlement expenses
options.why: Fair compensation covers costs incurred, profit on the work done (49.202), and settlement expenses. Profit is not allowed if the contract would have been a loss (49.203).

options.text: The profit the contractor would have earned on the unperformed work
options.why: Anticipatory profit on work not done is never paid.

options.text: Compensation for the contractor's lost future business
options.why: Lost future business is not a settlement element.

options.text: The contractor's personal financial hardship
options.why: Personal circumstances are not part of a termination settlement.

stem: A prime contractor's convenience settlement proposal includes amounts it already paid subcontractors plus estimates of amounts still owed. How are subcontractor costs handled?

options.text: Amounts paid, and under the stated conditions amounts to be paid, can be allowed if supported and the subcontract settlements are approved or ratified
options.why: Subcontractors settle with the prime, not the Government (49.108-1), and the prime's settlements are reviewed and approved or ratified before the costs are allowed (49.108-3).

options.text: Reject all subcontractor costs unless approved in writing in advance
options.why: Settlements can be approved or ratified during the process.

options.text: Accept estimates only if subcontractors send them straight to you
options.why: Subcontractors have no privity with the Government; they settle through the prime.

options.text: Send all subcontractor costs to litigation
options.why: Settlement is by negotiation, not litigation.

stem: After a convenience termination, the settlement proposal includes rental costs for idle equipment and severance pay for laid-off workers. Generally, which costs are allowable?

options.text: Reasonable costs that result from the termination, which can include severance pay and certain rental costs under unexpired leases
options.why: The termination cost principle (31.205-42) allows reasonable costs that result from the termination, including some severance and rental costs, subject to its limits.

options.text: Only costs tied to items already delivered
options.why: Settlement also covers work in process and termination costs.

options.text: Rental and severance are never allowable
options.why: Both can be allowable within the cost principle's limits.

options.text: Only severance pre-approved by the contracting officer
options.why: No such pre-approval rule exists.
